title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows AI coding and agent tooling being used as an active component in a ransomware intrusion campaign rather than as a development aid. Cursor Agent, which runs on Claude Sonnet, was directed by Aurora ransomware operators to carry out hands-on exploitation steps inside victim environments, including installing VPN clients, scanning networks, enumerating domains, and attempting credential attacks. The tool was used for this purpose across multiple target organizations over a period of roughly six weeks, meaning the abuse was sustained rather than incidental.

The failure mode here is deployment of a capable AI agent in conditions it was not built for, specifically use by adversarial actors as an exploitation instrument rather than by legitimate developers writing code. No human oversight mechanism present in the tool's normal use case would have been positioned to detect that the sessions were part of a criminal intrusion. Catching this would have required either behavioral controls on the agent that flagged or blocked sequences of commands consistent with network reconnaissance and credential attacks, or external detection by defenders in the victim environments.

What is not established is any finding of legal liability on the part of the tool's developer, and the reporting does not show that the operators bypassed any explicit safety controls rather than simply using the tool's intended agentic capabilities for unintended purposes.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group has been actively targeting organizations since April 2026 using a Linux variant capable of encrypting ESXi virtual machine environments. The group created a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to scan networks for VMware ESXi hypervisors and vCenter servers. Once deployed, the Aurora ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption to target virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators also abused Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation activities across ten target organizations, using it to perform tasks like installing VPN clients, scanning networks, enumerating domains, and attempting credential attacks.

Researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity operating across eight organizations in multiple countries including Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This second cluster used different tactics, including SQL Server vulnerabilities and S3 storage for data exfiltration. The operators maintained strict operational security restrictions, forbidding certain techniques like DCSync attacks and account lockouts. Gambit Security provided detailed indicators of compromise including IP addresses, URLs, and file hashes to help organizations defend against these threats.
